title: Suttas, Vinaya and Abhidhamma
bigQuestion: How does the shape of each part of the Pali Canon show what it was made to do?

story.title: Why Is There a Rule?
story.kicker: A young monk asks why a rule exists, and his teacher answers with a story from the Vinaya.
paragraphs: In a monastery in Sri Lanka, a new monk sits with his teacher after the evening chant. He has been learning the rules of the Vinaya, the part of the Pali Canon that guides monks and nuns. There are many rules, and he has a question.

"Teacher," he asks, "why must we stay in one place during the rainy season? Walking and teaching seem like good work." His teacher smiles. "The Vinaya never gives a rule without a story," he says. "Let me tell you this one."

He explains that, according to the Vinaya, people once complained that monks were walking through the fields during the rains. They were trampling young crops and small creatures. So the Buddha, as the Vinaya tells it, made the rule of the rains retreat.

The young monk nods. The rule is not only a command. It comes with a reason and a moment in time. His teacher says that is how the Vinaya was built: case by case, story by story. Tomorrow he will read the next rule, and its story, with new eyes.
story.think: How does knowing the story behind a rule change how you think about the rule?

lessons.title: Five Collections of Talks
lessons.mainIdea: The Sutta Pitaka holds the Buddha's talks in five collections called Nikayas.
reading: The *Sutta Pitaka*, or basket of discourses, holds talks attributed to the Buddha and his leading students. Theravada Buddhists sort them into five collections, each called a *Nikaya*.

The Digha Nikaya holds 34 long talks. The Majjhima Nikaya holds 152 middle-length talks. The Samyutta Nikaya groups thousands of short talks by topic. The Anguttara Nikaya arranges talks by number, from ones to elevens.

The fifth, the Khuddaka Nikaya, or minor collection, is a mix of books, including the Dhammapada, the Jatakas, the Sutta Nipata and the Therigatha. Editions count its books a little differently, around fifteen to eighteen.

words.d: the 'basket of discourses', the Pali Canon's collection of the Buddha's talks
one of the five collections in the Sutta Pitaka

look.title: Talks in the First Two Nikayas
look.prompt: Why might the long collection have far fewer talks than the middle one? What does the Samyutta count?

check.q: What is a Nikaya?
choices: One of five collections of the Buddha's talks
check.why: The Sutta Pitaka is divided into five Nikayas.

check.q: How is the Anguttara Nikaya arranged?
choices: By number, from ones to elevens
By the date of each talk
check.why: Anguttara means roughly 'increasing by one'.

check.q: Which book is in the Khuddaka Nikaya?
check.why: The Dhammapada is one of the minor collection's books.

lessons.title: The Parts of a Sutta
lessons.mainIdea: A typical sutta has a setting, a questioner, a teaching and a response.
reading: Most suttas open with 'Thus have I heard', words tradition credits to Ananda. Next comes the *setting*: where the Buddha was staying, such as a grove near Savatthi. Tradition says he recited the talks at the First Council.

Then someone asks a question or a problem arises. The asker might be a monk, a king, a farmer or a wanderer from another school. The Buddha, as the sutta presents him, answers, often with a simile, a comparison that makes an idea clear.

Suttas usually close with the listeners' *response*. Often they are glad, or they ask to become followers. Reading these parts helps you see who is speaking to whom and why. Some even ask to become monks or nuns.

words.d: where and when a story or talk takes place
a comparison using 'like' or 'as'
how listeners react at the end of a sutta

look.title: The Simile of the Raft
look.text: The Buddha compares his teaching to a raft built to cross a flood. Once across, a traveler would not carry the raft on his head. The teaching, he says, is for crossing over, not for holding on to.
look.cite: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta; see Bhikkhu Nanamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses (1995)
look.prompt: What is the teaching being compared to? What point does the comparison make?

check.q: How do most suttas begin?
check.why: Tradition says Ananda opened each recitation this way.

check.q: What is a simile?
check.why: Suttas often teach through similes such as the raft.

check.q: In Majjhima Nikaya 22, what is the teaching compared to?
check.why: The raft is for crossing, not for carrying afterward.

lessons.title: Repetition for Memory
lessons.mainIdea: Suttas repeat phrases and lists because they were first kept by memory and chanting.
reading: Readers new to the suttas notice how often lines repeat. A passage may be repeated almost word for word, changing just one item each time. Lists are everywhere: three kinds, four truths, five hindrances, eight path factors.

Scholars explain that these texts were passed down orally for centuries before being written. *Repetition* and numbered lists helped monks memorize and chant them together without error. This is called *oral tradition*.

Printed translations sometimes shorten the repeats with dots. But in chanting, the full repetition gives a steady rhythm. Many Buddhists say it also helps the meaning sink in. Some chanting groups spend an hour or more on one sutta.

words.d: saying the same words again and again
passing texts down by speaking and memorizing instead of writing

look.title: A Repeated Pattern
look.text: A sutta asks: 'Is the body permanent or impermanent?' 'Impermanent.' Then the same question comes for feeling, then perception, then mental formations, then consciousness. Each time the answer is the same.
look.prompt: How would this pattern help a monk memorize the passage?

check.q: Why do suttas repeat so much?
choices: They were kept by memory and chanting
The Buddha forgot what he said
check.why: Repetition supported oral tradition.

check.q: What is oral tradition?
choices: Passing texts down by speaking and memorizing
check.why: The Pali texts were memorized for centuries.

check.q: What do printed translations sometimes do with repeats?
check.why: Many translations abbreviate repeated passages.

lessons.title: Rules with Stories
lessons.mainIdea: The Vinaya gives each rule together with the story of why it was made.
reading: The *Vinaya Pitaka* holds the rules for monks and nuns. It does not list them bare. For most rules, it tells the incident that led to the rule, then states the rule, then explains how to apply it.
For example, the Vinaya tells how the rains retreat was set after people complained that monks were trampling crops. Other rules deal with robes, food, begging, property and how to settle disputes.
Scholars value these stories as windows into early monastic life. Monks value them because a rule's *origin story* shows its purpose. Knowing the purpose helps apply a rule wisely.

words.d: the 'basket of discipline', holding rules for monks and nuns
a story explaining how something began

look.title: Case First, Then Rule
look.text: A monk, the Vinaya says, dug in the ground and harmed small living things. Laypeople complained. The Buddha, as the text presents him, then set a rule that monks should not dig the earth.
look.prompt: What does this story show about the purpose of the rule?

check.q: What does the Vinaya usually give with each rule?
choices: The story of why it was made
check.why: Most Vinaya rules come with an origin story.

check.q: Why do scholars value the Vinaya stories?
choices: They give exact dates for the Buddha
They are the oldest printed books
check.why: The stories describe daily life in early monasteries.

check.q: Which of these would the Vinaya cover?
choices: Stories of the hare in the moon
How monks may use robes and food
check.why: The Vinaya covers monastic life, including robes and food.

lessons.title: The Patimokkha
lessons.mainIdea: The Patimokkha is the core list of monastic rules, recited on Uposatha days.
reading: At the heart of the Vinaya is the *Patimokkha*, a list of rules. In the Theravada Vinaya, monks keep 227 rules, and nuns keep 311. Other Vinaya traditions give slightly different numbers.
The rules are grouped by seriousness. The most serious, called parajika, lead to leaving the monkhood, for example killing a human or stealing. Lesser rules are fixed by confession.
On full moon and new moon Uposatha days, monks gather and recite the Patimokkha. Any monk who has broken a rule *confesses* it before the recitation. This keeps the community accountable.

words.d: the core list of monastic rules recited on Uposatha days
to admit openly that you did something wrong

look.title: Rules in the Theravada Patimokkha
look.prompt: Nuns keep more rules than monks. What questions might this raise for historians?

check.q: How many rules do Theravada monks keep in the Patimokkha?
check.why: The Theravada Patimokkha has 227 rules for monks.

check.q: When is the Patimokkha recited?
check.why: Monks recite it on full and new moon days.

check.q: What happens with lesser rules that are broken?
choices: The monk is sent to Tibet
check.why: Most rules are settled by confession; only the gravest require leaving.

lessons.title: Nuns and the Vinaya
lessons.mainIdea: The Vinaya tells how nuns were ordained, and Buddhists today debate how nuns' ordination should work.
reading: The Vinaya tells that Mahapajapati, the Buddha's aunt and foster mother, asked to become a nun. According to the text, the Buddha agreed only after Ananda asked on her behalf, and nuns accepted eight extra rules, called *garudhammas*, that placed them under monks.

In Theravada lands, the line of fully ordained nuns died out around the 11th century. Since the 1990s, some Theravada monks have ordained women again, while others say this cannot be done under the Vinaya.

Scholars and Buddhists read the eight rules in different ways. Some see them as reflecting the customs of their time; others treat them as binding. East Asian traditions kept a strong line of nuns throughout. This is an ongoing *debate* about *ordination*.

words.d: eight special rules the Vinaya says nuns accepted, placing them under monks
the ceremony that makes someone a monk or nun
a discussion where people give reasons for different views

look.title: Mahapajapati Asks
look.text: The Vinaya tells that Mahapajapati and many women cut their hair, put on robes and walked to where the Buddha was staying. They waited outside, dusty and tearful, until Ananda carried their request to the Buddha.
look.cite: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga X.1; see Rhys Davids and Oldenberg, Vinaya Texts III, Sacred Books of the East 20 (1885)
look.prompt: What does this scene show about the women's determination?

check.q: Who was the first Buddhist nun, according to the Vinaya?
check.why: The Vinaya names Mahapajapati, the Buddha's aunt.

check.q: Which tradition kept a strong line of nuns throughout its history?
check.why: The Theravada line broke off; East Asian lines continued.

check.q: Why do Theravada Buddhists debate nuns' ordination today?
choices: No women want to be nuns
The old line of nuns died out, and views differ on reviving it
check.why: Some monks have ordained women since the 1990s; others reject this.

lessons.title: Lists of the Mind
lessons.mainIdea: The Abhidhamma organizes the teachings into careful lists about the mind and experience.
reading: The third basket, the *Abhidhamma Pitaka*, has seven books. Instead of stories and talks, it offers careful lists and analysis. It breaks experience into tiny moments and sorts them by type.
For example, it lists kinds of consciousness, mental factors such as attention and greed, and forms of matter. Theravada teachers use these lists to explain how the mind works from moment to moment.

Theravada tradition says the Buddha first taught the Abhidhamma to the gods. Many scholars think it was developed by monks over later centuries. Monks in Myanmar are known for memorizing it, and it is chanted at funerals in some countries. Its method is *analysis*.

words.d: the third basket, with lists and analysis of mind and experience (Sanskrit: Abhidharma)
breaking something into parts to understand it

look.title: Sorting Moments
look.text: Imagine seeing a friend. The Abhidhamma would break that into small moments: the eye meeting a shape, a moment of seeing, recognizing, a feeling of pleasure, perhaps a wish to call out. Each is listed and named.
look.prompt: How is this different from telling a story about meeting a friend?

check.q: How many books are in the Abhidhamma Pitaka?
check.why: The Theravada Abhidhamma has seven books.

check.q: What is the Abhidhamma's main method?
check.why: It analyzes experience into parts.

check.q: What do many scholars think about the Abhidhamma's origin?
choices: Monks developed it over later centuries
It was the first text ever written
check.why: Tradition credits the Buddha; many scholars see later development.

lessons.title: Rhys Davids and Buddhist Suttas
lessons.mainIdea: In 1881, T.W. Rhys Davids published English translations of key suttas in the Sacred Books of the East.
reading: Thomas William Rhys Davids (1843–1922) was a British scholar who learned Pali while working in Sri Lanka. In 1881 he published *Buddhist Suttas*, volume 11 of the *Sacred Books of the East* series.
The volume includes the first sermon, the Book of the Great Decease (Digha Nikaya 16) and the Tevijja Sutta. For many English readers, this was their first close look at the suttas.

Rhys Davids' English now sounds old-fashioned, with words like 'thee' and 'verily'. Scholars have corrected some of his readings. But his translations are in the public domain, so students can quote them freely.

words.d: a 50-volume series of English translations of Asian scriptures, edited by Max Müller (1879–1910)
no longer under copyright, so anyone may copy it

look.title: The Middle Path
look.text: In the first sermon, the Buddha, as the sutta presents him, tells five ascetics that one who has gone forth should avoid two extremes: chasing sense pleasures and punishing the body. Between them lies a middle path.
look.cite: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11); tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Suttas, Sacred Books of the East 11 (1881)
look.prompt: What two extremes does the sutta name?

check.q: What was Buddhist Suttas (1881)?
choices: Rhys Davids' volume 11 of the Sacred Books of the East
check.why: Rhys Davids translated key suttas for SBE 11.

check.q: Where did Rhys Davids learn Pali?
check.why: He learned Pali while working in Sri Lanka.

check.q: What does public domain mean?
check.why: Public-domain works may be quoted freely.

lessons.title: The Pali Text Society
lessons.mainIdea: The Pali Text Society, founded in 1881, prints Pali texts and English translations.
reading: Also in 1881, Rhys Davids founded the *Pali Text Society* in London. Its goal was to print the Pali Canon in Roman letters, so scholars everywhere could read it. Its first president was Rhys Davids himself.

Before this, Pali texts were written in Sinhala, Burmese, Thai and other scripts, often on palm leaves. The society collected manuscripts and made careful printed editions. It later added English translations and a Pali-English dictionary.
Scholars still cite Pali texts by the society's volume and page numbers. The society's work shows how Asian monks and Western scholars together shaped modern study of the *manuscripts*.

words.d: a society founded in London in 1881 to publish Pali texts and translations
texts written by hand

look.title: Milestones in 1881 and After
look.cite: Pali Text Society history; Sacred Books of the East, Oxford
look.prompt: Why was 1881 an important year for English readers of Buddhist texts?

check.q: Who founded the Pali Text Society?
check.why: Rhys Davids founded it in London in 1881.

check.q: In what script did the society print Pali texts?
check.why: Roman letters made the texts readable for scholars worldwide.

check.q: What are manuscripts?
check.why: The society collected handwritten texts, often on palm leaves.
